overview:
The Central African Republic sits almost exactly in the middle of Africa, landlocked and far from any ocean. It is about the size of Texas but home to only around 5.5 million people, spread thinly across savanna and rainforest. The capital, Bangui, stands on the north bank of the Ubangi River, looking across the water to the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Neighbors also include Chad, Sudan, South Sudan, Congo, and Cameroon.

French and Sango are the official languages. Sango, which began as a trade language on the rivers, is special because nearly everyone in the country speaks it, a rare thing in Africa. Most people farm cassava, peanuts, and millet or fish the rivers, and the country's forests and soils hold diamonds, gold, and valuable timber. The Central African Republic is a republic with an elected president, but decades of coups and a civil war that began in 2012 have made it one of the poorest and least stable countries in the world, with UN peacekeepers based there since 2014.
landAndNature: Most of the country is a rolling plateau of savanna grasslands 600 to 900 meters high, broken by scattered hills and, in the northeast, the Bongo massif. Rivers flow in two directions: northward toward Lake Chad and southward into the Ubangi and Congo systems, and their waterfalls, like Boali Falls near Bangui, drop over rocky ledges. In the southwest the dense Congo rainforest begins. Dzanga-Sangha reserve is famous for the Dzanga Bai, a forest clearing where dozens of elephants gather to dig for salty minerals, and for western lowland gorillas that can be visited on foot. Manovo-Gounda St Floris park in the north once had huge herds but has suffered from poaching. Rain falls heavily from May to October.
peopleAndCulture: The Central African Republic has more than 80 ethnic groups, including the Gbaya, Banda, Mandjia, Sara, and Mbaka, plus the Aka, forest peoples of the southwest whose intricate polyphonic singing, with many voices weaving separate melodies, is recognized by UNESCO. Most people are Christian, with a Muslim minority. Cassava is the staple, pounded into a dough called gozo and eaten with sauces of greens, peanuts, or smoked fish, and caterpillars are a seasonal treat. Music blends drums, the balafon xylophone, and the sanza thumb piano with modern Congolese rumba. Soccer and basketball are the favorite sports. Colorful wax-print clothing and beautifully braided hairstyles are part of everyday style in Bangui.
history: Farming and iron-working peoples lived here more than 2,000 years ago, and mysterious stone monuments near Bouar are among the oldest in Central Africa. From the 1600s to the 1800s slave raiders from the north and traders from the coast devastated the region. France claimed the territory in the 1880s and ruled it as Ubangi-Shari, forcing people to gather rubber and cotton. A beloved independence leader, Barthélemy Boganda, died in a plane crash in 1959, a year before independence on August 13, 1960. Military ruler Jean-Bédel Bokassa seized power in 1966 and even crowned himself emperor in 1977 before being overthrown. More coups followed. Fighting between armed groups since 2012 has displaced more than a million people, though elections and peace talks continue.
funFacts: Sango is one of the few African languages spoken by almost the entire population of its country.
At Dzanga Bai, up to a hundred forest elephants may gather at once to drink mineral-rich water.
In 1977 ruler Jean-Bédel Bokassa spent a fortune on a coronation ceremony modeled on Napoleon's.
The Aka people can imitate the calls of forest animals so precisely that hunters use the sounds to lure game.
Boali Falls, about 50 meters high and 250 meters wide, is a popular picnic spot an hour from Bangui.
